nodes.label: Existing MARL evaluation suites do not treat generalization to novel situations as their primary objective.
A background population is the part of a multi-agent simulation that is imbued with agency, excluding the focal population of agents being tested.
Maximizing collective reward often produces policies that are less robust to novel social situations than the policies obtained by maximizing individual reward.

To perform well on Melting Pot's test scenarios, trained agents should be generalists. Division of labor is possible but works best when it self-organizes at test time, and where specialization is most important, successful populations should feature significant redundancy.
Ranking agents by skill is complicated and depends on how much each test scenario contributes to the overall score, and the authors' simple evaluation is far from the only option.

Prosocial OPRE and A3C matched regular OPRE and A3C in self-play but scored closer to random in test scenarios, an overfitting the authors attribute to prosocial agents learning only cooperation strategies and so becoming exploitable by defectors at test time.
Melting Pot uses reinforcement learning to reduce the human labor required to create novel test scenarios, which works because one agent's behavior is part of another agent's environment.
The results suggest that doing well on Melting Pot will require agents able to balance selfishness and prosociality contingently.
Agents that learn specialized policies expecting others to behave in a particular way form a division of labor that can create efficiency but also makes populations less robust.
Melting Pot reveals weaknesses in MARL algorithms that training performance alone does not show.
Solving Melting Pot's test scenarios seems to require agents that understand trust, generosity, forgiveness, reciprocity, stubbornness and deception.

Because the effectiveness of its bots advances with improvements in learning systems, Melting Pot will improve over time by reincorporating the latest agent technology into new background populations and test scenarios.
Agents sampled from a multi-agent population must generalize to interact with unfamiliar individuals not seen during training, who may be human, and pass a universalization test.
Every model tested has runs that lose coherence over a long horizon, including the strongest.
A long-horizon failure typically begins with the agent misreading its own operational state, after which it loops or abandons the task.
The breakdown is not explained by context length, because models degrade well after their memory is already full.
Giving an agent more memory made it perform worse, not better.
Every model tested had runs that ended in bankruptcy, however well it did on average.
Long-term coherence can be measured on its own by making each task simple and the horizon long.
LLMs gain far less from a larger time budget than humans do.
The human baseline rests on a single sample, so the variance that separates humans from models is not measured.
Capability profiles inferred with Measurement Layouts for Melting Pot contest entries predict the entries' future performance within the Melting Pot suite.

To infer the cooperation capabilities of Melting Pot contest entries, the authors construct a measurement layout: a hierarchical Bayesian model that estimates an entry's normalized score in different scenarios from the demands those scenarios impose.
For several Melting Pot contest submissions, both the assessor models and the Measurement Layouts have low predictive power.

Some high-scoring Melting Pot contest agents may succeed not because of their prosocial abilities but because of general competence, or an ability to complete tasks without the specific prosocial capabilities the measurement layouts capture.
The single top-ranked Melting Pot contest submission used a hand-crafted policy tuned to each substrate.

Several learning-based Melting Pot contest submissions show similarly high base-chance rates, suggesting that they too might have narrowly specialized for situations in which cooperation conferred no additional advantage.
The authors recommend that future competitions incorporate better-formulated meta-features to characterize task demands while avoiding duplicate demands.

Reducing the sparsity of the meta-features that annotate task demands would increase confidence in inferred capabilities and reduce the risk of competitors exploiting weaknesses in the evaluation framework.
Higher prosocial capability does not reliably accompany higher contest score.
Higher-scoring Melting Pot contest entries have significantly higher base-chance rates: they are more likely to perform better when prosocial demands are absent.

It is plausible that leading Melting Pot contest submissions gained much of their edge by excelling in scenarios that did not reward prosocial ability, thereby exploiting a weakness in the evaluation framework.
In the Melting Pot contest analysis, some inferred capabilities did not differentiate between submissions, possibly because the corresponding demands were sparsely present in the competition.
Whether the prosocial ability measurement layout transfers beyond Melting Pot to other social-AI evaluation suites is unresolved.
Future models could treat Melting Pot substrates as bias factors that influence the estimation of agents' latent abilities.
Traditional internet trust mechanisms assume static human-operated services and cannot meet the coordination needs of large-scale agent ecosystems.
State-of-the-art LLM agent frameworks exhibit prompt injection, sycophancy, hallucination, deception and misalignment.
Six trust models are available to inter-agent protocol design: Brief, Claim, Proof, Stake, Reputation and Constraint.
No single inter-agent trust mechanism is sufficient on its own.
High-impact agent actions should be gated by cryptographic proof and bonded stake rather than by reputation or self-declared claims.
Verification should be tiered to stakes: low friction where impact is negligible, relentless verification where it is high.
Reputation mechanisms presume a persistent identity with behavioral continuity, sanction sensitivity and costly non-fungibility.
Language model agents are assemblages of mutable modules, any of which may change their behavior.
Dissociativity leaves agents without grounding for identifiability, predictability, credibility and rehabilitability.
Reputation signals for dissociative agents become actively harmful rather than merely uninformative.
Identity-based, ex post, sanction-based governance is structurally inapplicable to dissociative agents.
Governance should target the operator and the protocol rather than the agent.
Identity and reputation are unsolved problems in technical AI governance.
How to assign accountability under fragmented identity is unresolved, and has been for centuries in the law that has tried longest.
How ex ante constraint mechanisms interact in practice has not been studied.
The binding constraint on AI is shifting from capability to coexistence.
Once a system tips into a degraded equilibrium, escaping it may be costly or impossible.
Decentralizing capability across many agents leaves the coordination problem in place, multiplies the points of failure and makes oversight harder.
The actual choice is between systems that acknowledge strategic interdependence in their design and systems that defer reckoning with it until deployment, when the dynamics are least tractable.
A superintelligence born of the solipsistic approach to AI design, however capable a task solver, is unlikely to be cooperative.
The authors expect solipsistic methods to remain effective in narrow domains; their argument targets sociotechnical settings where advanced AI deployment will be heavily exposed to response dynamics.

An individual system may be perfectly aligned with a specification of desired behavior and still take part in collective dynamics that produce harm, instability or illegitimacy, even without overt misuse.
A learning problem exhibits endogenous non-stationarity when deploying a policy changes the transition dynamics or reward proxy through the response adaptations of other agents.
The train-test-deploy gap is the systematic divergence between performance on exogenous historical data and performance on the endogenous data produced by responses to the deployed policy.
Keeping humans in the loop requires that they retain the skills, information and cognitive engagement needed to exercise meaningful authority, not only the formal authority to intervene.
The dominant AI research paradigm treats the world as an exogenous and stationary source of feedback.
Deploying an AI system induces endogenous non-stationarity, producing a train-test-deploy gap.
For an AI operating among other adaptive actors, the more aggressively it exploits historical regularities, the faster those actors adapt in ways that render the regularities obsolete.
A dynamic evaluation is one whose test distribution depends on the evaluated policy through adaptive counterparties.
No existing evaluation approach yet meets, in combination, all the requirements the authors set out for a valid dynamic evaluation.
The shift the authors call for entails treating institutions as design primitives that restructure incentives at the pace of the systems they govern.
Legitimacy constraints bound which solutions are admissible at all, rather than trading off against efficiency.
An AI decision that is technically correct is still delegitimized by the absence of due process.
Artificial Organizational Intelligence is an organization's capacity to make its own knowledge legible and governable.
The ethnographer's authority shifts from solitary immersion to maintaining intelligibility inside a networked architecture.
Participatory ethnography can include machines as collaborators in interpretation rather than tools of extraction, under rules and permissions that can be collectively governed.
The authors' method is a design-oriented, participatory ethnography whose research tools are built together with collaborators and field participants.

Building the loop is the authors' name for regulating AI through a local, group process: specifying where and how AI systems connect into existing systems, and deciding collectively on boundaries such as permissions.
Human oversight of automated decisions rarely corrects algorithmic bias and often works as a performative check that neither improves decisions nor redistributes responsibility.

The question for AI oversight is not whether a human is in the loop at the moment of decision but how the loop is built: how organizations set context, permissions and the flow of meaning between people and machines.
Building the loop does not answer questions of liability or regulation, though it opens organizational approaches, such as shared rules, to mitigating AI harms.
Telescope gathers research data by letting community members flag a message and then asking its author for consent before the message enters the dataset.
In the authors' deployment, consent worked as a live governance surface rather than a one-time form: a participant's revocation was enforced across the system as it happened.
Knowledge Organization Infrastructure is one architecture that makes Artificial Organizational Intelligence possible, by letting people connect and govern otherwise disparate sites of knowledge.
Artificial Organizational Intelligence is about organizations talking to themselves and to each other through regulated feedback loops, not about replacing them with AI.
Coordinated sensors, curators and machine agents free the ethnographer from the limit of what one person can perceive or track.
Knowledge Organization Infrastructure is a protocol for connecting disparate systems without homogenizing them.
Ethnography changes from observing an organization's hidden practices to building the loops that make them computable.
Most organizational routines are opaque to outsiders and only weakly documented inside the organization itself.
What formal manuals present as systematic procedure appears on the shop floor as situated improvisation.
Informal practices such as storytelling preserve diagnostic expertise that the official databases do not hold.
Artificial Organizational Intelligence means being able to address an organization itself rather than one of its representatives.
Under this infrastructure the stages of ethnography stop being sequential: a fieldnote can sync to a dataset at once, then be interpreted and fed back into the organization.

1.3 Authority and legitimacy for machine actors

links.because: Melting Pot's authors write that solving its test scenarios seems to require agents that understand trust, generosity, forgiveness, reciprocity, stubbornness and deception. Beyond the High Score infers such abilities for contest entries and finds that higher ability does not reliably accompany a higher score: some lower-scoring entries had significantly higher reciprocity and convention-following ability than some higher-scoring ones, and forgiveness did not differ between entries. A high contest score is not the same as solving the scenarios, so both can hold, but the contest's ranking did not reliably reward the abilities the scenarios are said to require.

Melting Pot's authors show that testing against unfamiliar background populations reveals weaknesses that training performance does not. Beyond the High Score finds that, in the Melting Pot contest, higher- scoring entries had significantly higher base-chance rates: they were more likely to perform better in scenarios where prosocial demands were absent. So a high test score can still come from scenarios that do not exercise the prosocial abilities the suite is built to test, and what the held-out test reveals depends on reading results per demand, not only in aggregate. A narrowing, not a contradiction.

Within one paper: higher-scoring entries having significantly higher base-chance rates, so that they are more likely to perform better when prosocial demands are absent, is one of the observations from which the authors judge it plausible that leading entries gained much of their edge in scenarios that did not reward prosocial ability.

Melting Pot's authors expect the suite to improve over time as the latest agent technology is reincorporated into new background populations and test scenarios. Beyond the High Score argues it is plausible that leading contest entries gained much of their edge by excelling in scenarios that did not reward prosocial ability, exploiting a weakness in the evaluation framework. Both can hold, but the second conditions the first: if it is right, improvement of the kind Melting Pot expects also depends on its test scenarios rewarding the prosocial abilities they are meant to measure, not only on stronger agents in its background populations.

Inter-Agent Trust Models puts Reputation among six mechanisms available to an agent ecosystem. Dissociative Identity states the precondition reputation runs on — persistent identity with behavioral continuity, sanction sensitivity and costly non-fungibility. That does not refute the comparison; it bounds where one of its six entries can be used at all.

Within one paper: reputation presupposing persistent identity, sanction sensitivity and costly non-fungibility is the premise; harm from reputation signals for dissociative agents is what follows when the presupposition fails.

Within one paper: agents being assemblages of mutable modules is the premise; the loss of grounding for identifiability, predictability, credibility and rehabilitability is the consequence argued from it.

Inter-Agent Trust Models demotes reputation: gate high-impact actions by Proof and Stake instead. Dissociative Identity goes further — for agents without persistent identity, reputation signals are actively harmful rather than merely weak. Same direction, stronger claim.

Tiering verification to stakes assumes there is a principal to verify and to sanction. Dissociative Identity argues identity-based ex post governance is structurally inapplicable to LM agents, which conditions where the tiering recommendation can apply rather than refuting it.
Within one paper: deployment inducing endogenous non-stationarity is the premise from which the insufficiency of current evaluation follows.

Solipsistic Superintelligence counts multi-agent testbeds, citing Melting Pot, as a step toward dynamic evaluation because they let the system interact with a population of agents, while holding that no current approach yet meets all of its requirements in combination. That bounds Melting Pot's expectation that folding improved agents into new background populations will keep the suite improving. Under this paper's definition, counterparties must update in response to the evaluated policy's behavior; whether a periodic refresh of background populations provides that is the drafter's inference, which the paper does not state about Melting Pot.
